per_panel_breakdown.root_cause_of_previous_failure: render_bench::build() gives its scene no backdrop (set_backdrop is called only later, for the primitive benchmark), so the frame under test takes glass_backdrop's live-blur branch. The §10 buckets were inside the attached-backdrop branch, so they could never run. They are now recorded at function entry, before the branch.
per_panel_breakdown.resolved_cause: profile::note_pixels pushed a new Row with calls: 1, and Timer::drop -> record added one per call, so every bucket note_pixels created read one call high. Seeding new rows with calls: 0 reconciles 2 + 1 = 3 against the outer glass_backdrop row.

shipped_frame_path.finding: render_bench built its scene without the glass backdrop Compositor::new attaches, so every full_frame number from §7-§11 timed glass_backdrop's live-blur fallback (20.33 ms), not the copy path the shipped desktop takes. Compositor::new has always attached a blur/saturate source; the benchmark had drifted from it.
evidence: src/litric-shell/src/desktop.rs Compositor::new: source = Rc::new(paper.glass_source(blur, saturation)); scene.set_backdrop(Some(source))
src/litric-shell/examples/render_bench.rs build() before this batch: let scene = wallpaper.clone(); (no set_backdrop)
same binary, same run: full_frame glass_backdrop 20.3 ms while primitive_glass_backdrop_panel, which attaches a backdrop, costs 1.92 ms for a 600x420 panel
shipped_frame_path.method: render_bench scene now attaches wallpaper.glass_source(desktop::glass_params(theme)) exactly as Compositor::new does; an extra scene, full_frame_live_blur, detaches the backdrop before timing the same frames, so both paths are measured by the same binary. 5 separate processes, 15 frames per scene each; median of the five per-process medians, min and max of those medians.

fill_round_rect_optimization.status: VERIFIED (composition only; golden-frame gate remains BLOCKED)
fill_round_rect_optimization.finding: fill_round_rect re-derived the rounded-rect centre, both half-extents and the clamped radius -- two divides and a min/max chain -- for every pixel it visited, then paid index()'s bounds check and multiply again to write the result. Its opaque core also ran the full three-channel float blend per pixel even though blend returns an opaque source unchanged at coverage 1.0.
fill_round_rect_optimization.change: src/litric-shell/src/canvas.rs: hoist the geometry once per call and the per-row terms once per row; split each row into the exact left-edge/core/right-edge runs the old per-pixel condition selected; write through a row slice and the blend free function; fill an opaque core with slice::fill; report visited pixels through profile::note_pixels.

fill_round_rect_blend_table.status: VERIFIED (composition only; golden-frame gate remains BLOCKED)
fill_round_rect_blend_table.finding: The residual fill_round_rect cost was the translucent core's per-pixel blend, not the edge square root: the same 600x420 panel costs 0.229 ms opaque and 2.756 ms at alpha 0.37, while the edge work is identical. The 2.527 ms difference over 220,384 core pixels (568x388) is the three-channel float blend at full coverage, about 11.5 ns/px.
fill_round_rect_blend_table.change: src/litric-shell/src/canvas.rs: for a translucent core of at least 1024 clipped pixels, build a 256-entry table once per call with blend(0xFF000000|d<<16|d<<8|d, color, 1.0); the core loop then takes the R byte of table[r], the G byte of table[g] and the B byte of table[b]. Same blend function, same arithmetic, same rounding, so the pixels are identical. Small translucent cores keep the direct blend; opaque cores keep slice::fill. render_bench gained primitive_fill_panel_translucent as the control.
